Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Britain's Prince William is starting a two-month attachment with the Royal Navy on Monday, part of the future king's continued experience with various branches of the military, the Ministry of Defense said Saturday. Prince William and his father, Prince Charles, at his graduation from the Royal Air Force in April. William, 25, will spend the first part of his attachment on a basic sea safety course training in sea survival, firefighting and ship damage repair, according to the ministry. If William passes the course, as expected, he will join the HMS Iron Duke in the Caribbean, the department said. The ship's function is to support overseas British territories in the event of a hurricane and to carry out counter-narcotic operations. The prince, who will be called Sub Lieutenant Wales in the Navy, is expected to spend time aboard a frigate, a mine hunter, a submarine and helicopters during his attachment, which ends August 1, the Ministry of Defense said. William completed a four-month attachment with the Royal Air Force this year and received his pilot's wings upon graduating in April. He learned to fly three different aircraft during the attachment and is known as Flying Officer Wales within the RAF. William is also a second lieutenant in the British Army, where he serves in the Blues and Royals regiment of the Household Cavalry. The attachments are designed to provide the prince with military experience for when he becomes head of the armed forces as king. "When he becomes king, he needs to know his armed forces -- instinctively be very familiar with them -- and so he is doing this visit to the Royal Navy," said Rear Adm. Bob Cooling, the assistant chief of naval staff. William's father, Prince Charles, had a five-year career in the navy in the 1970s. Charles served on the guided missile destroyer HMS Norfolk and two frigates before qualifying as a helicopter pilot and joining a naval air squadron that operated from the aircraft carrier HMS Hermes. Prince Charles spent his last nine months in the navy in 1976 in command of the coastal minehunter HMS Bronington. William's uncle Prince Andrew served 22 years in the Royal Navy as a helicopter pilot, seeing active service during the Falklands War between Britain and Argentina in 1982. Queen Elizabeth II's husband, Prince Philip, William's grandfather, spent more than 13 years in the Royal Navy. He saw active service throughout World War II and was in Tokyo Harbor when Japan surrendered.

His Army role gave him experience of troop leadership, discipline and the operational culture of one of Britain’s most historic regiments.

He later spent time with the Royal Air Force, including pilot training and familiarisation with RAF operations. His RAF experience was designed to broaden his understanding of air power and the work of service personnel across the armed forces. William would go on to develop a particularly close association with aviation, later training as a helicopter pilot and serving in search and rescue.

The forthcoming Royal Navy period will complete a tri-service introduction similar to the kind of broad military grounding expected of senior royals with formal links to the armed forces. While the attachment is not intended to mark the start of a long-term naval career, it will allow William to gain direct insight into naval life, including shipboard routines, maritime operations and the demands placed on sailors and officers.

The move also places William in a long royal tradition of naval service. Several senior members of the Royal Family have served at sea, with the Navy playing a particularly prominent role in the careers of Prince Philip, Prince Charles and Prince Andrew.

Prince Philip, the Duke of Edinburgh, had one of the most distinguished royal naval careers of the modern era. He joined the Royal Navy before the Second World War after training at the Royal Naval College, Dartmouth, and served during the conflict in the Mediterranean and Pacific. He saw action aboard ships including HMS *Valiant* and was mentioned in dispatches for his role during the Battle of Cape Matapan in 1941. Philip later served as first lieutenant of HMS *Wallace*, becoming one of the youngest officers in the Navy to hold such a post at the time. His active naval career ended after the accession of Queen Elizabeth II, though he retained a lifelong association with the service.

Prince Charles also served in the Royal Navy after earlier RAF training. He joined the Navy in the 1970s and served aboard several ships, including HMS *Norfolk*, HMS *Minerva*, HMS *Jupiter* and HMS *Hermes*. He qualified as a helicopter pilot and, in 1976, took command of the coastal minehunter HMS *Bronington*. His period in command is often cited as a formative part of his military career, giving him direct responsibility for a ship and crew before he left active service later that year.

Prince Andrew pursued the most substantial naval career of the Queen’s sons. He joined the Royal Navy in 1979 and trained as a helicopter pilot. During the Falklands War in 1982, he served aboard HMS *Invincible*, flying Sea King helicopters in missions that included anti-submarine duties, casualty evacuation and decoy operations. He remained in the Navy for many years after the conflict, later commanding the minehunter HMS *Cottesmore* and continuing in active service until 2001.

William’s naval attachment therefore carries both practical and symbolic significance. Practically, it will broaden his understanding of the three armed services. Symbolically, it reinforces the long-standing relationship between the monarchy and the Royal Navy, a bond shaped by wartime service, command at sea and generations of royal involvement in military life.

For William, the experience will add another layer to a military résumé that already includes Army officer training and RAF flying experience. For the Royal Navy, it will be another moment in a centuries-old association with the Crown — one that has helped define the public service of several generations of the Royal Family.
